# Results

Values in this section populate when the pre-registered analysis executes; every table below is rendered from the analysis code with its final structure, and cells display as pending until model training completes. No value in this section is estimated, assumed or illustrative.

## Severity skill

@tbl-severity reports severity-estimation skill per severity stratum for the two deep learning models and the SWIR change baseline on identical stand cells: root-mean-square error, relative RMSE normalised by the stratum mean of the reference severity, mean absolute error, and Theil's U with its bias, variance and covariance proportions.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-severity
#| tbl-cap: "Severity estimation error per severity stratum and model, from block spatial cross-validation. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
strata_lab <- c("0-0.01", "0.01-0.03", "0.03-0.05", "0.05-0.10",
                "0.10-0.20", ">0.20")
models <- c("TempCNN", "Transformer", "SWIR baseline")
sev_shell <- expand.grid(Stratum = strata_lab, Model = models,
                         KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
sev_shell[c("RMSE", "rRMSE", "MAE", "U_Theil", "U_bias", "U_var", "U_cov")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(sev_shell, right = c("RMSE","rRMSE","MAE","U_Theil","U_bias","U_var","U_cov"))
```

## Detection skill

@tbl-detection reports the confusion-matrix summary per stratum: user's and producer's accuracy and the primary metric, recall at 0.90 precision, with fold-wise dispersion. @tbl-h1 carries the H1 test: the fold-wise paired difference in the primary metric between each deep model and the baseline within the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum, its block-bootstrap confidence interval, the one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank statistic, and the McNemar cell-level check. The detectability floor of each model is the lowest stratum whose primary metric exceeds the pre-registered threshold.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-detection
#| tbl-cap: "Detection skill per severity stratum and model: user's accuracy (UA), producer's accuracy (PA), and recall at 0.90 precision (R90, the pre-registered primary metric), with fold-wise standard deviation. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
det_shell <- expand.grid(Stratum = strata_lab, Model = models,
                         KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
det_shell[c("UA", "PA", "R90", "R90_sd")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(det_shell, right = c("UA","PA","R90","R90_sd"))
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-h1
#| tbl-cap: "Test of H1 in the 0.01 to 0.10 severity stratum: fold-wise paired difference in recall at 0.90 precision against the SWIR baseline, block-bootstrap 95% confidence interval, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank p-value, and McNemar chi-squared on paired cell-level detections. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
h1_shell <- data.frame(Model = c("TempCNN", "Transformer"),
                       Delta_R90 = ".", CI95 = ".", Wilcoxon_p = ".",
                       McNemar_chisq = ".", Floor = ".")
fmt_tbl(h1_shell, right = c("Delta_R90","CI95","Wilcoxon_p","McNemar_chisq","Floor"))
```

## Onset dating

@tbl-onset reports onset-year error under the two supervision regimes, testing H2: mean absolute error and root-mean-square error in years, the share of predictions falling within the label bracket, and the fold-wise paired difference between triangulated and single-epoch supervision.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-onset
#| tbl-cap: "Onset-year estimation error by model and supervision regime (triangulated two-epoch intervals against single-epoch labels), with the H2 paired test. Values pending execution of the pre-registered analysis."
onset_shell <- expand.grid(Model = c("TempCNN", "Transformer"),
                           Supervision = c("Triangulated", "Single-epoch"),
                           KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
onset_shell[c("MAE_yr", "RMSE_yr", "In_bracket", "Delta_MAE", "Wilcoxon_p")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(onset_shell, right = c("MAE_yr","RMSE_yr","In_bracket","Delta_MAE","Wilcoxon_p"))
```

## Independent evaluation

@tbl-independent reports agreement with the untouched severity reference of @Zwieback_2024 in the Talkeetna to Byers Lake footprint, using only fold models whose training excluded the footprint: the same error slate as @tbl-severity at 90 m and 30 m support, alongside the published within-study errors of the reference itself for context, which are not directly comparable and are marked as such.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-independent

ind_shell <- expand.grid(Support = c("90 m", "30 m"), Stratum = strata_lab,
                         KEEP.OUT.ATTRS = FALSE)
ind_shell[c("RMSE", "rRMSE", "MAE", "U_Theil")] <- "pending"
fmt_tbl(ind_shell, right = c("RMSE","rRMSE","MAE","U_Theil"))
```

@tbl-progression compares reconstructed annual outbreak area against the aerial survey record, reported as descriptive correspondence: mapped area, surveyed area, their ratio, and the intersection-over-union of the footprints per year.


# Discussion

## Detection floor

[Pending: interpretation of @tbl-severity, @tbl-detection and @tbl-h1.] The decisive comparison is confined to the 0.01 to 0.10 stratum, where @Zwieback_2024 found stand-scale SWIR change uninformative and where roughly ninety percent of the region's beetle-killed spruce resides. If the paired difference in @tbl-h1 excludes zero, the detectability floor of freely available imagery drops below the published 0.1 threshold and the fraction of the outbreak visible to open-data monitoring rises accordingly; if it does not, the result consolidates the case that sub-metre imagery is a hard requirement for low-severity beetle mapping in mixed boreal forest, itself a finding with operational cost implications. Either outcome resolves the transfer question left open between the defoliator system of @Perbet_2024, where temporal deep learning recovered partial disturbance from Landsat, and the bark beetle system here, whose multi-year fade [@Hicke_2024; @Kautz_2024] presents a slower but weaker annual signal.

## Temporal supervision

[Pending: interpretation of @tbl-onset.] The triangulation design tests a claim with reach beyond this outbreak: that a second high-resolution label epoch buys more onset-dating skill than any refinement of a single-epoch label set, because it converts static labels into interval-censored ones and exposes annotation errors through cross-epoch consistency. The expected one to two year lag between spectral change and onset [@Perbet_2024] bounds what any optical method can date; @tbl-onset quantifies how much of that bound the interval supervision recovers. The four-cut footprint, where the labels of @Zwieback_2024 interleave with both mosaic epochs, indicates the ceiling available where label epochs are dense.

## Limitations

Five limitations are known by design. First, crown labels derive from visual interpretation of sub-metre imagery, so fully occluded dead spruce under closed deciduous canopy are absent from both training and reference data, and severity is accordingly a minimum estimate in dense mixed stands [@Zwieback_2024]. Second, the harmonized Sentinel-2 surface reflectance archive over Alaska begins effectively in 2019, so the first three outbreak years rest on the sparser Landsat record, and onset estimates for stands that died early carry wider intervals. Third, the independent severity reference is itself a model product with documented error structure, not ground truth; agreement with it bounds, rather than establishes, map accuracy. Fourth, mortality agent is inferred from context, not confirmed by ground observation, and other agents of spruce death are conflated with beetle kill at unknown but presumed low rates. Fifth, the study area is one outbreak in one region; transfer to the Kenai Peninsula, to Interior Alaska or to other *Dendroctonus* systems is untested and, on the evidence of cross-system transfer failures elsewhere [@Kautz_2024], should not be presumed.

## Operational implications

[Pending: contingent on @tbl-h1 and @tbl-progression.] The aerial detection survey remains the only annual statewide observation system, and nothing here replaces it; the question is what a free satellite complement adds. A model whose floor sits below 0.1 severity would flag dispersed mortality the surveys under-record, at annual cadence, over unflown terrain, for the cost of compute alone, with the reconstructed progression in @tbl-progression indicating how faithfully such a system would have tracked this outbreak had it run from 2016. The label pipeline is the transferable asset: statewide sub-metre mosaics now recur, and each new epoch extends the interval-censored label set without new fieldwork.

# Conclusion

[Pending: quantitative sentences follow the pre-registered analysis.] This study asks a bounded question with a decade of consequence behind it: how much of a spruce beetle outbreak can freely available satellite data see? Prior work fixed the answer at severities above 0.1, leaving most beetle-killed trees in this landscape invisible to open-data monitoring. The design assembled here tests whether temporal deep learning moves that boundary, using only open data end to end: Cloud Score+ screened Sentinel-2 composites, crown labels digitised on public statewide mosaics, onset intervals triangulated between mosaic epochs, and an independent published severity product as referee. Whatever the direction of the result, the study delivers the first annually resolved, openly reproducible record of the 2016 to 2025 Southcentral Alaska outbreak at stand scale, a labelled dataset positioned to grow with each statewide mosaic epoch, and a pre-registered benchmark against which subsequent methods, sensors and regions can be measured.

# Data availability

All inputs are publicly retrievable; the download script, checksums and provenance manifest are in the project repository. The severity rasters of @Zwieback_2024 are archived at doi:10.5281/zenodo.8423568, the crown labels at doi:10.5281/zenodo.10569990 and the trained network at doi:10.5281/zenodo.10569975; the latter two are distributed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 licence, while the severity rasters carry no declared licence and are used for independent evaluation only, pending clarification with the author. Aerial detection survey data are distributed by the United States Forest Service as public-domain works, and Sentinel-2, Landsat and elevation data are open under their respective public licences. The Maxar mosaics of the State of Alaska Geoportal are accessible for non-commercial use by streaming and are not redistributed here.
